claim: Systemic toxicity is a major challenge in the development of therapeutics.
source: Systemic toxicity is a major challenge in the development of therapeutics.
evidence: This is a general statement about therapeutic development challenges presented in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Cell-type-specific targeting is needed to improve on-target efficacy while reducing off-target toxicity.
source: Consequently, cell-type-specific targeting is needed to improve on-target efficacy while reducing off-target toxicity.
evidence: This is a logical consequence stated in the abstract based on established therapeutic development principles.

claim: BRAID is a cell-targeting system whereby an active molecule is divided into two inactive or less active parts that are subsequently brought together via a bridging receptor on the target cell.
source: Here, we describe a cell-targeting system we have termed BRAID (BRidged Activation by Intra/intermolecular Division) whereby an active molecule is divided into two inactive or less active parts that are subsequently brought together via a so-called 'bridging receptor' on the target cell.
evidence: This is the main conceptual claim of the manuscript describing the BRAID system.

claim: A multivalent WNT agonist molecule divided into two inactive components assembled from different epitopes via the hepatocyte receptor βKlotho induces signaling specifically on hepatocytes.
source: This concept was validated using the WNT/β-catenin signaling system, demonstrating that a multivalent WNT agonist molecule divided into two inactive components assembled from different epitopes via the hepatocyte receptor βKlotho induces signaling specifically on hepatocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4 showing hepatocyte-specific signaling.

claim: The BRAID approach may allow activation of multiple signaling pathways where desirable.
source: This approach, in principle, also allows action upon a combination of different signaling pathways simultaneously, potentially providing additive or synergistic effects.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications of the approach.

claim: The BRAID approach has broad application potential for other receptor systems.
source: This approach has broad application potential for other receptor systems.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the generalizability of the approach.

claim: Receptor-mediated signaling is fundamental to cell–cell communication, regulation of cellular growth/differentiation, maintenance of tissue function/homeostasis, and regulation of injury repair.
source: Receptor-mediated signaling is fundamental to cell–cell communication, regulation of cellular growth/differentiation, maintenance of tissue function/homeostasis, and regulation of injury repair.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about receptor signaling.

claim: Nature achieves cell-specific response selectivity through various mechanisms such as cell-specific receptors, ligand gradient, short-range ligands, and direct cell–cell contacts.
source: When a cell-specific response is necessary, nature achieves that selectivity through various mechanisms such as cell-specific receptors, ligand gradient, short-range ligands, and direct cell–cell contacts.
evidence: This is based on established biological knowledge about cell signaling mechanisms.

claim: Most ligand receptor systems have pleiotropic effects due to the broad expressions of receptors on multiple cell types.
source: However, most ligand receptor systems have pleiotropic effects due to the broad expressions of receptors on multiple cell types.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge of receptor biology.

claim: It is often difficult to identify differences between normal and diseased cells for a particular signaling pathway of interest.
source: In addition, it is often difficult to identify differences between normal and diseased cells for a particular signaling pathway of interest, making it challenging, if not impossible, to modulate that signaling pathway selectively in either diseased or normal cells.
evidence: This is a statement about challenges in therapeutic development based on general knowledge.

claim: Cell-targeted agonists are more complex to design compared with cell-targeted antagonists.
source: Compared with cell-targeted antagonists, cell-targeted agonists are more complex to design.
evidence: This is a general statement about drug design complexity.

claim: Agonist molecules are subject to stringent requirements in terms of affinity, epitope, and geometry.
source: In addition to cell targeting, agonist molecules are also subject to stringent requirements in terms of affinity, epitope, and geometry (Dickopf et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dickopf et al., 2020.

claim: The 'chimeric activators' concept involves attaching a cell-targeting arm to either the wild-type ligand or a mutated ligand with reduced affinity toward the signaling receptor.
source: Previous efforts to engineer cell-selective growth factors and cytokines have employed various approaches, such as the 'chimeric activators' concept (Cironi et al., 2008), where a cell-targeting arm ('targeting element') is attached to either the wild-type ligand or a mutated ligand with reduced affinity toward the signaling receptor ('activity element').
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cironi et al., 2008.

claim: The chimeric activators approach has been applied to signaling pathways based on erythropoietin.
source: Such an approach has been applied to several signaling pathways, such as those based on erythropoietin (Taylor et al., 2010; Burrill et al., 2016), interferons (Cironi et al., 2008; Garcin et al., 2014), and interleukin-2 (Ghasemi et al., 2016; Lazear et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taylor et al., 2010 and Burrill et al., 2016.

claim: The chimeric activators approach has been applied to signaling pathways based on interferons.
source: Such an approach has been applied to several signaling pathways, such as those based on erythropoietin (Taylor et al., 2010; Burrill et al., 2016), interferons (Cironi et al., 2008; Garcin et al., 2014), and interleukin-2 (Ghasemi et al., 2016; Lazear et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cironi et al., 2008 and Garcin et al., 2014.

claim: The chimeric activators approach has been applied to signaling pathways based on interleukin-2.
source: Such an approach has been applied to several signaling pathways, such as those based on erythropoietin (Taylor et al., 2010; Burrill et al., 2016), interferons (Cironi et al., 2008; Garcin et al., 2014), and interleukin-2 (Ghasemi et al., 2016; Lazear et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ghasemi et al., 2016 and Lazear et al., 2017.

claim: Up to 1000-fold selectivity has been achieved using a mutated ligand in the chimeric activators approach.
source: While some selectivity has been achieved by attaching a targeting arm to a wild-type ligand, up to 1000-fold selectivity has been achieved using a mutated ligand (Garcin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Garcin et al., 2014.

claim: The chimeric activators approach is based on the cooperativity concept where mutations weaken the affinity of a natural ligand to its receptor.
source: The 'chimeric activators' approach is based on the cooperativity concept, where mutations that weaken the affinity of a natural ligand to its receptor are selected as the 'activity element.'
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism underlying the chimeric activators approach.

claim: The mutant 'activity element' alone displays a significantly right-shifted dose–response curve in an activity assay for both target and non-target cells that express the signaling receptors.
source: Due to this weakened affinity, the mutant 'activity element' alone displays a significantly right-shifted dose–response curve (i.e., lower potency) in an activity assay, for both target and non-target cells that express the signaling receptors.
evidence: This is an explanation of the functional consequence of weakened affinity in the chimeric activators approach.

claim: When the 'targeting element' is tethered to the mutant 'activity element,' the 'targeting element' helps increase the local concentration of the mutant 'activity element' on the desired target cell surface.
source: When the 'targeting element' is tethered to the mutant 'activity element,' the 'targeting element' helps increase the local concentration of the mutant 'activity element' on the desired target cell surface.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism by which the chimeric activators approach achieves selectivity.

claim: Identifying the appropriate mutations that achieve the precise reduction of affinity to be rescued by the 'targeting element' is not trivial.
source: While conceptually elegant, identifying the appropriate mutations that achieve the precise reduction of affinity to be rescued by the 'targeting element' is not trivial.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical challenges of the chimeric activators approach.

claim: In some cases of the chimeric activators approach, while the potency could be rescued, the maximal signaling strength remained compromised, resulting in a partial agonist.
source: In some cases, while the potency could be rescued, the maximal signaling strength remained compromised, resulting in a partial agonist.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of the chimeric activators approach based on general knowledge.

claim: Most literature examples of the chimeric activators approach report a modest tenfold separation between target vs. non-target cells.
source: In addition, the selectivity is not exquisite, with most literature examples reporting a modest tenfold separation between target vs. non-target cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about the selectivity achieved by chimeric activators based on literature review.

claim: Inactive pro-drugs that require tumor-associated proteases for activation show promising results as a cell-targeting strategy.
source: Additional strategies that show promising results have also been reported; for example, inactive pro-drugs that require tumor-associated proteases for activation (Puskas et al., 2011; Skrombolas et al., 2019); complementation of two inactive components via targeted assembly in trans (Banaszek et al., 2019) and passive enrichment on the target cell leading to colocalization of monomeric subunits (Mock et al., 2020) or inactive 'split' components (Quijano-Rubio et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Puskas et al., 2011 and Skrombolas et al., 2019.

claim: Complementation of two inactive components via targeted assembly in trans shows promising results as a cell-targeting strategy.
source: Additional strategies that show promising results have also been reported; for example, inactive pro-drugs that require tumor-associated proteases for activation (Puskas et al., 2011; Skrombolas et al., 2019); complementation of two inactive components via targeted assembly in trans (Banaszek et al., 2019) and passive enrichment on the target cell leading to colocalization of monomeric subunits (Mock et al., 2020) or inactive 'split' components (Quijano-Rubio et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Banaszek et al., 2019.

claim: Passive enrichment on the target cell leading to colocalization of monomeric subunits shows promising results as a cell-targeting strategy.
source: Additional strategies that show promising results have also been reported; for example, inactive pro-drugs that require tumor-associated proteases for activation (Puskas et al., 2011; Skrombolas et al., 2019); complementation of two inactive components via targeted assembly in trans (Banaszek et al., 2019) and passive enrichment on the target cell leading to colocalization of monomeric subunits (Mock et al., 2020) or inactive 'split' components (Quijano-Rubio et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mock et al., 2020 and Quijano-Rubio et al., 2023.

claim: The WNT pathway is highly conserved across species and crucial for embryonic development as well as adult tissue homeostasis and regeneration.
source: The WNT pathway is highly conserved across species and crucial for embryonic development as well as adult tissue homeostasis and regeneration (Nusse and Clevers, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nusse and Clevers, 2017.

claim: WNT-induced signaling through β-catenin stabilization is achieved by the ligand binding to frizzled (FZD) and the low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein (LRP) families of receptors.
source: WNT-induced signaling through β-catenin stabilization has been widely studied and is achieved by the ligand binding to frizzled (FZD) and the low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein (LRP) families of receptors.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of WNT signaling.

claim: There are 19 mammalian WNTs, 10 FZDs (FZD1-10), and 2 LRPs (LRP5 and LRP6).
source: There are 19 mammalian WNTs, 10 FZDs (FZD1-10), and 2 LRPs (LRP5 and LRP6).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the number of WNT pathway components based on established knowledge.

claim: WNTs are highly hydrophobic due to lipidation, which is required for them to function.
source: WNTs are highly hydrophobic due to lipidation, which is required for them to function, and they are promiscuous, capable of binding and activating multiple FZD and LRP pairs (Janda et al., 2012; Kadowaki et al., 1996; Dijksterhuis et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Janda et al., 2012; Kadowaki et al., 1996; Dijksterhuis et al., 2015.

claim: WNTs are promiscuous, capable of binding and activating multiple FZD and LRP pairs.
source: WNTs are highly hydrophobic due to lipidation, which is required for them to function, and they are promiscuous, capable of binding and activating multiple FZD and LRP pairs (Janda et al., 2012; Kadowaki et al., 1996; Dijksterhuis et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Janda et al., 2012; Kadowaki et al., 1996; Dijksterhuis et al., 2015.

claim: Elucidating the functions of individual FZDs in tissues has been hampered by difficulties in producing the ligands and their lack of receptor and tissue selectivity.
source: Elucidating the functions of individual FZDs in tissues has been hampered by difficulties in producing the ligands and their lack of receptor and tissue selectivity.
evidence: This is a statement about challenges in WNT research based on general knowledge.

claim: Recent breakthroughs in the development of WNT-mimetic molecules have largely resolved the production and receptor-specificity challenges.
source: Recent breakthroughs in the development of WNT-mimetic molecules have largely resolved the production and receptor-specificity challenges (Janda et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2019; Miao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Janda et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2019; Miao et al., 2020.

claim: Tissue selectivity has been partly achieved by tissue injury, as damaged tissues seem more sensitive to WNTs.
source: Although tissue selectivity has been partly achieved by tissue injury (damaged tissues seem more sensitive to WNTs; Xie et al., 2022), the ability to target WNTs to specific cells and tissues would be a significant technical and therapeutic advancement.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xie et al., 2022.

claim: WNT mimetics reported so far are all bispecific and can simultaneously bind to FZDs and LRPs.
source: The WNT mimetics reported so far are all bispecific and can simultaneously bind to FZDs and LRPs, and their optimal stoichiometry (at least for the antibody-based molecules) are tetravalent bispecific (2:2 format), requiring two FZD binders and two LRP binders in the same molecule to achieve efficient signaling (Tao et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tao et al., 2019 and Chen et al., 2020.

claim: The optimal stoichiometry for antibody-based WNT mimetics is tetravalent bispecific (2:2 format), requiring two FZD binders and two LRP binders in the same molecule to achieve efficient signaling.
source: The WNT mimetics reported so far are all bispecific and can simultaneously bind to FZDs and LRPs, and their optimal stoichiometry (at least for the antibody-based molecules) are tetravalent bispecific (2:2 format), requiring two FZD binders and two LRP binders in the same molecule to achieve efficient signaling (Tao et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tao et al., 2019 and Chen et al., 2020.

claim: Two FZD binders alone do not signal.
source: We have taken advantage of the fact that two FZD binders alone and two LRP binders alone do not signal.

claim: Two LRP binders alone do not signal.
source: We have taken advantage of the fact that two FZD binders alone and two LRP binders alone do not signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Efficient WNT/β-catenin signaling requires two FZD-binding domains and two LRP-binding domains in one molecule.
source: It is important to note that efficient WNT/β-catenin signaling requires two FZD-binding domains and two LRP-binding domains in one molecule (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2020.

claim: FGF21 is an endocrine hormone produced by the liver that regulates metabolic homeostasis.

claim: One particular agonistic βKlotho antibody binds to a different epitope on βKlotho from FGF21 and does not compete with FGF21 binding.
